lessons.title: The periodic table: groups 0, 1 and 7
lessons.summary: Discover how the periodic table is organised, why Mendeleev's version worked, and how electron structure explains the patterns in the noble gases, alkali metals and halogens.
objectives: I can explain how elements are arranged in the modern periodic table and why Mendeleev left gaps.
I can use electronic structure to explain why elements in the same group react in similar ways.
I can describe and explain the trends in reactivity down group 1 and down group 7.
I can predict the outcome of displacement reactions between halogens and halide salts.

activities.title: How the table is arranged
activities.content:
## Reading the periodic table

The modern periodic table lists elements in order of **atomic number** (the number of protons). It is called *periodic* because similar properties turn up again and again at regular intervals.

- A vertical column is a **group**. Elements in a group have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**, which is why they behave in similar ways.
- A horizontal row is a **period**. Moving along a period, each element has one more proton and one more electron than the last, and a new period starts each time a new shell begins to fill.

The group number tells you the outer-shell electrons: sodium is in group 1 and has 1 outer electron; chlorine is in group 7 and has 7. (Group 0 elements have full outer shells.)

A zig-zag line separates **metals** on the left and centre from **non-metals** on the right. Most elements are metals. Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions, or share electrons in covalent bonds.

activities.title: Before Mendeleev, and why his table worked
activities.content:
## A short history

Early in the 1800s, chemists tried arranging elements in order of **atomic weight**. These lists put some elements in groups where their behaviour did not fit, and nobody had a way to deal with elements not yet discovered.

In 1869 **Dmitri Mendeleev** did two clever things:

1. He **left gaps** where he believed undiscovered elements belonged, and predicted their properties. When gallium and germanium were later found, they matched his predictions closely.
2. He was willing to **swap the order** of a few elements so that they sat with elements of similar chemistry, even if this broke the strict order of atomic weight.

The swaps made sense once **isotopes** were understood. Atomic weight depends on the mix of isotopes, so it does not always increase in step with the number of protons. Ordering by **atomic number** instead of atomic weight removed the problem, and this is how the modern table is built.

question.text: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
question.hint: Think about what he believed would eventually fill them.
question.explanation: Mendeleev left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered so that known elements could sit with others that had similar properties. He predicted the properties of the missing elements.

options.text: For elements that had not yet been discovered
Because he ran out of elements to include
options.feedback: The gaps were deliberate and had predicted properties.

options.text: To separate the metals from the non-metals
Because some elements were too dangerous to include

activities.title: Group 0: the noble gases
activities.content:
## Group 0

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are the **noble gases**. Each has a **full outer shell** (helium has 2 electrons; the rest have 8), so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. That makes them **unreactive** and they exist as single atoms (monatomic).

Trend down the group:

| Property | Trend going down |
|---|---|
| Relative atomic mass | increases |
| Boiling point | increases |
| Density | increases |

Boiling point rises because larger atoms have more electrons, so the weak forces between atoms are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.

Uses rely on their lack of reactivity: helium fills balloons (low density, non-flammable), argon protects the filament in some light bulbs, and neon glows in advertising signs.

activities.title: Worked example: predicting a boiling point
activities.content:
**The boiling points of some noble gases are: neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, xenon −108 °C. Estimate the boiling point of krypton.**

Krypton sits between argon and xenon in the group. Boiling point increases down group 0, so krypton should boil at a temperature **between −186 °C and −108 °C**. A sensible estimate is about **−150 °C**. (The real value is −153 °C.)

The important skill is spotting the direction of the trend and placing the missing value between its neighbours.

question.text: True or false: the noble gases are unreactive because they have a full outer shell of electrons.
question.hint: What does an atom gain by reacting? Do noble gas atoms need it?
question.explanation: True. A full outer shell is a stable arrangement, so noble gases do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.

options.text: True
False

activities.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
activities.content:
## Group 1

Lithium, sodium and potassium (plus rubidium, caesium and francium) are the **alkali metals**. Each atom has **one electron in its outer shell**, which it loses easily to form a **+1 ion**. They are soft enough to cut with a knife and have low densities: lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water.

**Reaction with water** produces a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$

The solution is alkaline (hence the name), and the fizzing is hydrogen. Potassium reacts so vigorously that the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame.

**Reaction with chlorine** gives a white metal chloride, e.g. $2K + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2KCl$.

**Reactivity increases down the group.** The outer electron is further from the nucleus in a larger atom, and it is shielded by more inner shells, so the attraction holding it is weaker and the electron is lost more easily. Melting and boiling points **decrease** down the group.

question.text: Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium does.
question.hint: Compare where the outer electron sits in each atom and how strongly the nucleus holds it.
question.explanation: Potassium atoms are larger, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells. The attraction to the nucleus is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and potassium reacts faster.

markScheme.criterion: Outer electron is further from the nucleus / more shells / more shielding in potassium
So the outer electron is held less strongly and is lost more easily

activities.title: Group 7: the halogens
activities.content:
## Group 7

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are the **halogens**. They are non-metals with **seven outer electrons** and exist as **diatomic molecules** ($F_2$, $Cl_2$, $Br_2$, $I_2$).

At room temperature:
- fluorine is a pale yellow gas
- chlorine is a green gas
- bromine is a red-brown liquid
- iodine is a grey solid that gives a purple vapour

So **melting and boiling points increase** down the group, as the molecules get bigger and the forces between them get stronger.

A halogen atom gains one electron to form a **−1 halide ion** (e.g. $Cl^-$), or shares an electron in a covalent bond with another non-metal.

**Reactivity decreases down the group.** This is the opposite of group 1, and the reason is the mirror image: in a larger atom the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is **harder to attract an extra electron** in.

activities.title: Worked example: halogen displacement
activities.content:
**Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium bromide. What happens?**

A more reactive halogen will **displace** a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. Chlorine is above bromine in group 7, so chlorine is more reactive.

$Cl_2 + 2KBr \rightarrow 2KCl + Br_2$

The colourless solution turns **orange-brown** because bromine is formed.

**Now try bromine water added to potassium chloride.** Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so **no reaction** occurs and the solution stays the same colour.

Useful table:

| Added halogen | KCl(aq) | KBr(aq) | KI(aq) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | no change | orange (Br₂) | brown (I₂) |
| Bromine | no change | no change | brown (I₂) |
| Iodine | no change | no change | no change |

question.text: Which of the following mixtures will produce a reaction? Select all that apply.
question.hint: A halogen only displaces a halogen below it in the group.
question.explanation: Chlorine displaces iodide and bromine displaces iodide. Iodine cannot displace chloride, and bromine cannot displace chloride, because they are less reactive.

options.text: Chlorine added to sodium iodide solution
Bromine added to potassium iodide solution
Iodine added to sodium chloride solution
options.feedback: Iodine is the least reactive of the three, so it cannot displace chloride.

options.text: Bromine added to potassium chloride solution
options.feedback: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so no displacement happens.

question.text: Complete the word equation and the description.

metadata.blanksText: sodium + water → sodium ___ + ___. The solution formed turns universal indicator ___ because it is alkaline.

question.hint: The gas is the one that squeaky-pops with a lit splint.
question.explanation: Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. Sodium hydroxide is an alkali so universal indicator turns purple (blue is also accepted).

question.text:
Astatine is at the bottom of group 7.

(a) Predict the state of astatine at room temperature and explain your prediction. (2 marks)

(b) A student adds astatine to a solution of sodium chloride. Explain, in terms of electrons, why no reaction takes place. (2 marks)
question.hint: Use the trends: state and reactivity both follow a clear pattern down the group.
question.explanation: (a) Solid, because melting and boiling points increase down group 7 and iodine, above it, is already a solid. (b) Astatine is less reactive than chlorine: its outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it attracts an extra electron less strongly and cannot take an electron from a chloride ion.

markScheme.criterion: Because melting/boiling points increase down the group
Astatine's outer shell is further from the nucleus / more shielded, so it attracts electrons less strongly
So astatine is less reactive than chlorine and cannot displace it / cannot gain an electron from chloride

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Elements are ordered by **atomic number**; groups share the same number of outer electrons.
- Mendeleev left **gaps** and swapped some elements so properties matched; isotopes explain the swaps.
- **Group 0**: full outer shells, unreactive, boiling points rise down the group.
- **Group 1**: one outer electron, form +1 ions, react with water to give hydroxide + hydrogen, **more reactive down the group**.
- **Group 7**: seven outer electrons, diatomic, form −1 ions, **less reactive down the group**; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt.

practiceQuestions.text: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing…
practiceQuestions.hint: It is the number that identifies an element.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The modern table is ordered by atomic number, the number of protons.

options.text: atomic number
atomic weight
options.feedback: That was the early approach and it caused problems.

options.text: density
melting point

practiceQuestions.text: An element has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Which group of the periodic table is it in?
practiceQuestions.hint: Count the electrons in the outer shell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The outer shell holds 7 electrons, so the element is in group 7 (it is chlorine).

practiceQuestions.text: Arrange these group 1 metals from least reactive to most reactive.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Lithium is at the top of the group and least reactive; potassium is lower and more reactive than sodium.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each halogen to its appearance at room temperature.
practiceQuestions.hint: The halogens go gas → liquid → solid down the group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Chlorine is a green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey solid.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: bromine can displace chlorine from a solution of sodium chloride.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so bromine cannot displace it.

options.text: True
False

metadata.blanksText: A group 1 atom loses one electron to form an ion with a charge of ___. A group 7 atom gains one electron to form an ion with a charge of ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Losing a negative electron leaves a positive charge.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Group 1 metals form +1 ions; group 7 halogens form −1 ions.

practiceQuestions.text: The boiling points of helium and argon are −269 °C and −186 °C. Which statement best explains the difference?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the size of the atoms and the forces between them.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Argon atoms are larger with more electrons, so the forces between atoms are stronger and more energy is needed to boil it.

options.text: Argon atoms are larger so the forces between atoms are stronger
Argon has a full outer shell but helium does not
Helium forms molecules but argon does not
Argon is more reactive than helium

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties.
practiceQuestions.hint: What decides how an atom reacts?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elements in a group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and it is the outer electrons that take part in reactions.

markScheme.criterion: Outer electrons determine chemical reactions / how an element reacts

practiceQuestions.text:
Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium iodide.

(a) Describe what you would observe. (1 mark)

(b) Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (2 marks)

(c) State why chlorine is able to displace iodine. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: Iodine in solution is brown. The two products are potassium chloride and iodine.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The colourless solution turns brown as iodine forms. (b) Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. (c) Chlorine is more reactive than iodine because it is higher in group 7.

markScheme.criterion: Correct reactants and products: Cl2 + KI → KCl + I2
Chlorine is more reactive than iodine / higher in the group

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are trends going DOWN group 1? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Down group 1, reactivity increases and melting point decreases. The number of outer electrons stays at one, and the atoms get larger, not smaller.

options.text: Reactivity increases
Melting point decreases
Number of outer electrons increases
options.feedback: Every group 1 element has exactly one outer electron.

options.text: Atoms get smaller

practiceQuestions.text: Mendeleev sometimes placed an element slightly out of order of atomic weight. Why did he do this?
practiceQuestions.hint: Mendeleev thought properties mattered more than a strict order of weights.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mendeleev swapped the order of a few elements so that each one sat in a group with elements that had similar chemical properties. He trusted the pattern of properties more than the measured atomic weights.

options.text: So that each element was grouped with others that had similar properties
Because he arranged the elements by atomic number instead
options.feedback: Atomic number was not known in Mendeleev's time; it explained his swaps only later.

options.text: To make every row of the table the same length
Because those elements had not yet been discovered
options.feedback: Undiscovered elements were given gaps, not swapped positions.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: neon forms ions easily because its atoms need to gain one more electron to fill their outer shell.
practiceQuestions.hint: Neon is in group 0. Is its outer shell already full?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Neon has the electronic structure 2,8, so its outer shell is already full. It has no need to gain, lose or share electrons, which is why it is so unreactive.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Caesium is near the bottom of group 1. Explain, in terms of electrons, why caesium reacts more violently with water than sodium does.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the distance of the outer electron from the nucleus in each atom and how much it is shielded by inner shells.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A caesium atom has more shells than a sodium atom, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner electrons. The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and caesium reacts more violently.

markScheme.criterion: Outer electron is further from the nucleus / more shells / more shielding in caesium
So the outer electron is held less strongly and is lost more easily

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following mixtures will produce a displacement reaction? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Reactivity decreases down group 7, and a halogen can only displace a less reactive halogen from its salt.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromide. Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodide. Iodine is the least reactive of the three, so it cannot displace bromide, and bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine from chloride.

options.text: Chlorine added to potassium bromide solution
Bromine added to sodium iodide solution
Iodine added to lithium bromide solution
options.feedback: Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace bromide.

options.text: Bromine added to lithium chloride solution
options.feedback: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so no displacement takes place.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the word equation and the observation.

metadata.blanksText: lithium + water → lithium ___ + ___. During the reaction the piece of lithium ___ on the surface of the water because it is less dense than water.

practiceQuestions.hint: All group 1 metals form the same type of compound with water and give off the same gas. Think about what a low-density solid does in water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Lithium reacts with water to form lithium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Lithium is less dense than water, so it floats on the surface as it fizzes.

practiceQuestions.text:
Fluorine is at the top of group 7.

(a) Predict the state of fluorine at room temperature and explain your prediction. (2 marks)

(b) Fluorine is bubbled through a solution of sodium bromide. Explain, in terms of electrons, why a reaction takes place. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Melting and boiling points change in a regular way down group 7, and so does reactivity. Think about how strongly a small halogen atom attracts an extra electron.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Fluorine is a gas, because melting and boiling points increase down group 7 and chlorine, just below fluorine, is already a gas at room temperature. (b) Fluorine is more reactive than bromine: its outer shell is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it attracts an extra electron more strongly. Fluorine atoms take electrons from bromide ions, displacing bromine.

markScheme.criterion: Because melting/boiling points increase down the group (so are lowest at the top)
Fluorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus / less shielded, so it attracts an electron more strongly
So fluorine is more reactive than bromine and displaces it / takes an electron from bromide ions
